<description>
{
 "summary": "Optimizes primitive serialization and serialized size calculation across Bitcoin Core's stream, crypto, and serialization primitives. It adds single-byte write and read overloads using fixed-extent spans (std::span<..., 1>) across AutoFile, DataStream, VectorWriter, and SHA-256 contexts to bypass general buffer allocations and memcpy calls. In addition, it consolidates primitive integer serialization using C++20 concepts and if constexpr, allowing SizeComputer to advance byte offsets directly without performing endianness conversions.",
 "problem": "Generic serialization routines impose small per-element overheads that accumulate during high-volume operations like block serialization and Initial Block Download (IBD). Single-byte writes (e.g. booleans, VarInt prefix bytes, and int8 types) invoke general stream buffering or memcpy, while SizeComputer pointlessly computes endian transformations when only the byte length matters.",
 "evidence": [
  "Author's nanobench results report SerializeBlock latency improving from ~195 \u00b5s to ~174 \u00b5s on AppleClang and from ~867 \u00b5s to ~615 \u00b5s on GCC 13, with SizeComputerBlock dropping from ~12.0 \u00b5s to ~10.2 \u00b5s on AppleClang and ~30.9 \u00b5s to ~25.6 \u00b5s on GCC.",
  "Author's 3-run hyperfine IBD benchmark to block height 880,000 reports bitcoind running '1.02 \u00b1 0.02 times faster' (mean wall time reduced from 33,647s to 33,062s)."
 ],

<discussion_facts>
open objections:
- maflcko (member), usefulness, open: AutoFile single-byte write optimizations are not hit during production IBD because reads and writes are already buffered
- sedited (contributor), scope, open: unclear benefit of specializing single-byte writes in crypto/sha256 adds complexity
support:
- theuni (member): no verdict word; These are nice optims
- sedited (contributor): no verdict word; This looks ok, albeit that I'm seeing more modest performance improvements on my end.
- sedited (contributor): no verdict word; I think block serialization being fast could be useful for future kernel users. Reading and de-serializing blocks is one of the common operations I'd expect outside of just pure block validation.
</discussion_facts>

<category name="tests" title="Test infrastructure">
## Covers

The machinery of testing rather than tests of a particular area: the
functional test framework and runner, unit test utilities, the fuzzing
harnesses and corpora, benchmarks, linters, sanitizer configuration,
and fixes for flaky tests whose cause is in the framework. A test that
pins the behavior of one area (a wallet migration test, a p2p relay
test) belongs to that area, not here. The Tests and Fuzzing labels are
a prior, but a labeled PR whose tests are about one area goes to that
area instead.

## What matters here

Signal first: fixes for flaky or misleading tests, since a red CI that
nobody trusts hides real failures. Then coverage of high-risk code paths
that the fuzzers or functional tests do not reach, especially
consensus, mempool policy, and p2p message handling. Then framework
capabilities that unblock tests other areas need. Then test speed, which
every contributor pays for on every run. Then cleanliness of the test
code.

Adding tests for their own sake ranks low; adding a test that catches a
realistic regression ranks high.

<category name="utils" title="Utilities (logging, arguments, libraries)">
## Covers

Shared infrastructure used across the node: logging, argument and
settings handling, startup and shutdown sequencing, error and result
types, serialization, randomness and cryptographic primitives, threading
and locking utilities, and the vendored subtrees (secp256k1, leveldb,
minisketch, univalue, crc32c). The Utils/log/libs label is a strong
prior.

Not utils: a logging or settings change whose point is one area's
behavior (that area); the kernel API (kernel).

## What matters here

Unlike most categories, internal improvements are the subject here, so
judge them on their own terms. Correctness and safety of primitives
first: randomness, cryptography, serialization, locking, and shutdown
behavior are where subtle bugs become node-wide problems. Then
subtree updates that carry security or correctness fixes. Then
user-facing behavior of configuration and logging: confusing options,
lost log lines, startup failures. Then reductions in a burden every
other area carries: an error-handling pattern that simplifies many call
sites, a logging API that makes categories consistent. Then cosmetic
consistency.
